claim_details.claim: Whether pregnant women should follow a vegan diet is a subject of genuine scientific debate. On one hand, several scientific societies—including the U.S. Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics—have issued official statements backing the safety of well-planned vegan diets for all stages of life, including pregnancy, provided that nutrient needs are met through a variety of plant foods and reliable sources of vitamin B12 and D ; research suggests such diets may even offer benefits like a lower risk of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes maternal or infant mortality a 2015 study concluded that vegan-vegetarian diets may be considered safe during pregnancy if nutritional requirements are met

On the other hand, Belgium's Royal Academy of Medicine recommended that pregnant women avoid vegan diets due to unavoidable nutritional shortcomings and potential irreversible harms to the developing brain the vegan keto diet in particular is explicitly noted as unsuitable for pregnant women

The key consensus across sources is that a vegan diet can be safe during pregnancy only if it is well-planned, includes fortified foods and supplements (particularly B12 and D) is carefully monitored by a healthcare provider—highlighting that planning and nutritional adequacy are paramount

claim_details.claim: The Word of Wisdom, received as a revelation in 1833, was not initially given as a commandment but as 'a principle with promise'

The first formal step toward making it a universal commandment came on September 9, 1851, when President Brigham Young proposed at a general conference that all Church members formally covenant to keep the Word of Wisdom — a motion unanimously accepted by the Church — at which point it became binding as a commandment for all members
Over the following decades, adherence remained a matter of personal covenant rather than a strict membership requirement, though it gradually became a criterion of orthodoxy under Heber J. Grant

The most significant formal mandatory requirement came in 1919–1921, when the First Presidency under President Grant made observing the Word of Wisdom a requirement for receiving a temple recommend by 1915 it was already required for young or middle-aged men to be ordained to the priesthood
